items.label: f01-pagesize-or-zero
items.front: Settings code reads `const pageSize = settings.pageSize || 10;` and a user has saved `pageSize: 0`. What does the app use, and why?
items.back: It uses 10: 0 is falsy, so || discards the user's value. Fix: `settings.pageSize ?? 10`, which falls back only on null/undefined. Keep || for real boolean logic.

items.label: f04-delete-204-json
items.front: A deletePost helper ends with `return res.json();` after a DELETE. Deletes succeed on the server but the UI shows an error every time. What is happening?
items.back: DELETE often returns 204 No Content; parsing an empty body as JSON throws, turning a successful delete into a failure. Fix: check res.ok and do not parse the body of a DELETE (or check for 204 first).

items.label: f03-fetch-no-res-ok
items.front: A getTodo helper does `const res = await fetch(url); return res.json();` with a .catch on the caller. For a missing id the server answers 404, yet the catch never fires. Why?
items.back: fetch only rejects on network failure; a 404/500 still resolves. Without `if (!res.ok) throw new Error(...)` the error body is parsed as data. Fix: check res.ok before res.json().

items.label: f02-shallow-copy-nested
items.front: Code copies a profile with `const shallow = { ...original }` and then sets `shallow.address.city = "NYC"`. A bug report says the original profile's city changed too. Why?
items.back: Spread copies one level; `address` is a shared nested object, so the write lands in both. Fix: `structuredClone(original)` (or copy the nested level too) when the copy must be independent.

Only `date`, now an ISO string rather than a Date; the function and the undefined field are dropped
Nothing at all, because JSON.stringify throws when an object contains a function value
All three keys, with `fn` turned into its source text and `missing` turned into null

items.prompt: updatePost sends only `{ title: "Edited" }`. Why does the lab use PATCH for that request rather than PUT?

choices.text: PATCH is idempotent and PUT is not, so retrying a PUT could apply the title change twice
PUT cannot carry a JSON body, so the title would have to be moved into the query string
PUT is reserved for creating new resources, so it would add a second post instead of editing one
PATCH means change only the listed fields, while PUT means replace the whole resource with the body that was sent

PUT is reserved for creating new resources, so it would add a second post instead of editing one
PATCH means change only the listed fields, while PUT means replace the whole resource with the body that was sent

items.explanation: Problem 31: PATCH = change only these fields; PUT = replace the whole resource. CRUD: Create=POST, Read=GET, Update=PUT/PATCH, Delete=DELETE.

render() only re-draws when it receives a new array reference, so the rollback would be skipped
The in-place flip would make saveFn run twice, so the server would receive the toggle a second time
The catch block would never run, because mutating an array cancels the pending saveFn promise

items.prompt: In fetchWithRetry, what would the caller observe if the final `throw lastError;` were deleted and every attempt failed?

Node would crash with an unhandled rejection, because the errors were caught but never logged
The last error would still reach .catch, because the catch block inside the loop already rethrows it
The loop would retry forever, because nothing would stop it once the attempts were used up

The loop would retry forever, because nothing would stop it once the attempts were used up

items.explanation: Problem 32: the catch inside the loop swallows each failure (lastError = err); `throw lastError` after the loop is what surfaces the final error once all attempts are exhausted.

choices.text: filter deep-clones every remaining todo, so later edits cannot reach the old objects
splice cannot remove items by id, only by value, so it would delete the wrong todo
filter builds a new array and leaves the original list untouched, which is the update shape React state expects
filter is faster than splice because it skips the index lookup that splice needs

Returning false reports that nothing was deleted and lets the caller decide whether a missing id is actually an error
remove re-inserts the task when it returns false, so callers can retry the delete safely

items.prompt: A page loads three users with `await Promise.all([...])` and one request rejects. What does the page get, and which tool keeps the two successful users?

choices.text: Promise.all retries the failed request once and then resolves; allSettled skips the retry and rejects
Promise.all resolves with the two users and an undefined slot; allSettled would only add the error message
Promise.all waits for all three and then rejects with an array of errors; allSettled would throw sooner
Promise.all rejects with that one error and returns no results; Promise.allSettled reports every outcome so the two successes can be kept

Promise.all resolves with the two users and an undefined slot; allSettled would only add the error message

Promise.all rejects with that one error and returns no results; Promise.allSettled reports every outcome so the two successes can be kept

items.explanation: Problem 28: if ANY promise rejects, Promise.all rejects immediately with that error; allSettled returns fulfilled/rejected records you can filter.

items.prompt: `timer.start()` passes `function () { console.log(this.seconds); }` to setTimeout and logs undefined. Why does switching the callback to an arrow function fix it?

choices.text: An arrow function has no `this` of its own and inherits it from start(), where `this` is the timer object
Arrow functions are automatically bound to the object they are written in, like a class method
Arrow functions run synchronously inside start(), so they read `seconds` before the timer fires
setTimeout calls arrow callbacks with the original object as an argument instead of as `this`

setTimeout calls arrow callbacks with the original object as an argument instead of as `this`

items.explanation: Problem 23: `this` is set by how a function is called (the timer machinery calls the plain function); arrows capture `this` lexically. `.bind(this)` is the other fix.

Faster than Promise.all, because consecutive awaits avoid the overhead of combining three promises
